title: Oven-steamed hāngī-style pork, chicken and vegetables
steps: Heat the oven to 160 C. Season the pork and chicken generously with salt and pepper.
Line a deep roasting tin with two layers of baking paper, then foil, leaving a generous overhang. Put the onion and the meat in the base.
Pour in the water. Lay a wet clean tea towel over the meat, fold the foil over to seal, and put the tin in the oven for 90 minutes.
Open the parcel carefully and add the kumara, potato and pumpkin on top, with the cabbage last. Lay the wet towel back over and seal tightly again.
Cook for a further 90 to 120 minutes until the pork is tender and the vegetables are soft. Rest for 15 minutes before opening and serve everything together.
notes: This is a home-oven imitation. A real hāngī is cooked in a pit by people who know the tradition, and the smoky earth flavour cannot be reproduced exactly.

title: Pork bone boil-up with doughboys

ingredients.note: bones with meat, such as ribs or neck bones

steps: Put the pork bones and onion in a large pot, cover with about 2.5 litres of water and bring to the boil. Skim off the foam.
Simmer gently for about 90 minutes until the meat is tender. Season with salt and pepper.
Add the potato, kumara and pumpkin and cook for 20 minutes until nearly soft.

Make the doughboys: mix flour, baking powder and salt, then stir in the oil and enough water to make a soft dough. Spoon walnut-sized pieces into the simmering broth, cover, and cook for 10 to 12 minutes.
Stir in the watercress for the last minute. Serve in deep bowls with the broth.
notes: Traditional boil-up uses puha, which can be hard to find; watercress or silverbeet is an easy substitute.

title: Potato-starter rēwena bread

ingredients.note: peeled and diced, boiled until soft, cooking water kept
warm potato cooking water, topped up with water
a pinch of dried yeast to help the rise

steps: Make the starter at least 2 days ahead. Mash the cooled potato with its cooking water, then stir in 100 g flour and the teaspoon of sugar to make a thick batter. Cover loosely and leave somewhere warm (about 24 C) for 2 to 3 days, stirring once a day, until bubbly and sour-smelling.
Mix the starter with the 500 g flour, sugar, salt and enough lukewarm water to form a soft dough. Knead for 8 to 10 minutes until smooth and stretchy.
Put in a greased bowl, cover, and leave in a warm place for 4 to 5 hours until about doubled.
Shape into a loaf and place in a greased 900 g tin. Cover and rise for 1 to 2 hours more until puffy.
Bake at 200 C for 15 minutes, then reduce to 180 C for 25 to 30 minutes until deeply golden and hollow-sounding. Cool on a rack.
notes: Without added yeast the rise is slow. If the starter seems sluggish, the pinch of yeast helps. Keep any leftover starter in the fridge and feed it with flour and water.

title: Fried bread
steps: Mix the flour, yeast, sugar and salt, then add the warm water and mix to a soft dough. Knead for 5 minutes.
Cover and leave in a warm place for 1 hour until puffy.
Roll or stretch the dough to about 2 cm thick and cut into 10 to 12 squares or rounds.
Heat the oil in a deep pan to 175 C. Fry the dough pieces a few at a time for about 2 minutes per side until puffed and deep golden.
Drain on paper towel and serve hot with butter and jam, or with a savoury stew.

title: Roasted kūmara wedges
steps: Heat the oven to 220 C.
Toss the kūmara with the oil, salt and pepper on a large tray in a single layer.
Roast for 35 to 40 minutes, turning once, until the edges are caramelised and a knife slides in easily.
notes: Good with a squeeze of lime or alongside roast meat. Red and orange kūmara varieties have a drier, nuttier texture than gold ones.

title: Strawberry and kiwifruit pavlova
steps: Heat the oven to 150 C and mark a 20 cm circle on baking paper on a tray.
Whisk the egg whites to stiff peaks. Add the sugar one spoonful at a time, whisking well between additions, until the meringue is thick and glossy and the sugar has dissolved.
Fold in the cornflour and vinegar. Heap onto the circle and shape into a round with a slight dip in the middle.
Put it in the oven and immediately lower the temperature to 120 C. Bake for 75 minutes.
Turn the oven off and leave the pavlova inside with the door shut until completely cool.
Just before serving, top with the whipped cream and fruit.
notes: Make it on a dry day. A few cracks on top are normal.

title: Honeycomb hokey pokey
steps: Line a 20 cm square tin with baking paper and measure out the baking soda before you start.
Heat the sugar, golden syrup and water in a large, deep pan over medium heat, stirring only until the sugar dissolves.
Boil without stirring for 6 to 8 minutes until it is a deep golden colour (about 150 C on a sugar thermometer).
Remove from the heat, whisk in the baking soda quickly (it will foam up a lot) and pour straight into the tin without spreading.
Cool completely, about 1 hour, then break into pieces. Store in an airtight tin.
notes: Hot sugar causes serious burns; use a large pan and take care when it foams.

title: Whitebait fritters
steps: Beat the eggs with the flour, salt and pepper until smooth, then gently fold in the whitebait.
Melt some of the butter in a frying pan over medium heat.
Spoon in the mixture in 4 to 6 patties and cook for 2 minutes per side until set and golden; they cook very quickly.
Serve right away with lemon, or between slices of buttered bread.
notes: Do not overcook; whitebait go rubbery.

title: Bluff oysters natural
steps: Keep the oysters chilled until you open them. Discard any that are open and will not close, or smell bad.
Hold an oyster in a folded cloth, hinge towards you. Work the tip of an oyster knife into the hinge, twist to pop it, and slide the blade along the top shell to release the muscle.
Lift off the top shell, loosen the oyster from the bottom shell, keeping the juices.
Arrange on crushed ice and serve with lemon and pepper.
notes: Eat shortly after opening. Pregnant people and those with weakened immunity should avoid raw shellfish.

title: Cheese and onion rolls
steps: Heat the oven to 200 C and line a tray with baking paper.
Mix the cheese, evaporated milk, grated onion, salt and pepper into a thick, spreadable paste.
Flatten each slice slightly with a rolling pin, spread a layer of filling over, and roll up tightly.
Butter the outside of each roll and place seam side down on the tray.
Bake for 10 to 12 minutes until golden and crisp, then serve hot.
